items.title: The Normal Curve
items.body: Bell-shaped, symmetric about mean \(\mu\). \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Approximately 68%/95%/99.7% within 1/2/3 standard deviations.

items.title: Standardising
items.body: \(Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)\). Use \(Z\)-tables (standard normal) to find probabilities.

items.title: Inverse Normal
items.body: Given probability, find the value. \(P(X<a)=p\Rightarrow a=\mu+z\sigma\) where \(z=\Phi^{-1}(p)\).

items.title: Finding μ or σ
items.body: Set up two equations from given probabilities, solve simultaneously for unknown parameters.

items.title: Normal Approximation
items.body: To Binomial \(B(n,p)\): if \(n\) large, \(np>5\), \(n(1-p)>5\): use \(N(np,np(1-p))\) with continuity correction \(\pm0.5\).

body.en: If \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\): standardise with \(Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\) where \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). Use tables (or calculator) for \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\leq z)\). Key symmetry: \(P(Z\leq -z)=1-P(Z\leq z)\). For inverse normal: given a probability, find the corresponding \(x\) value using \(x=\mu+z\sigma\).

Probabilistic Normalization & Moment Structure: Every probability model is governed by total probability conservation: \(\sum_x P(X=x) = 1\) for discrete random variables and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\) (with \(f(x) \ge 0\)) for continuous density functions. Expected value \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) acts as a linear operator (\(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y]\)), whereas variance scales quadratically and adds for independent variables: \(\operatorname{Var}(aX \pm bY) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

body.en:
Variance vs Standard Deviation: Cambridge notation specifies \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\). When standardising \(Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\), remember to divide by \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\), NOT by \(\sigma^2\).

Negative z-values and tables: Standard normal tables provide \(\Phi(z)\) only for \(z > 0\). By symmetry: \(\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)\). For lower-tail probabilities \(P(Z < -1.25) = 1 - \Phi(1.25)\).

Continuity correction (Normal approx to Binomial): When approximating discrete \(X \sim B(n, p)\) by continuous \(Y \sim N(np, np(1-p))\):
• \(P(X \ge a) \to P(Y > a - 0.5)\)
• \(P(X > a) \to P(Y > a + 0.5)\)
• \(P(X \le a) \to P(Y < a + 0.5)\)
• \(P(X = a) \to P(a - 0.5 < Y < a + 0.5)\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Normal Distribution)

body.en:
Why Variance Scales as \(a^2\) and Independent Variances Always Add: By definition, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \mu_Y)^2]\). For \(Y = aX - bW\) with independent \(X, W\), subtracting its mean \(\mu_Y = a\mu_X - b\mu_W\) gives:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[(a(X - \mu_X) - b(W - \mu_W))^2\right] = a^2\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)^2] - 2ab\,\operatorname{Cov}(X,W) + b^2\mathbb{E}[(W-\mu_W)^2] \]

Because independence implies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, W) = 0\), the cross term vanishes and \((-b)^2 = +b^2\), proving \(\operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(W)\). Uncertainty compounds whether random variables are added or subtracted.

Problem (Medium): A normal random variable \( C \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu = 44, \sigma^2 = 9) \) is observed at \( q = 47 \). Calculate the standardized score \( z = (q - \mu)/\sigma \).

Step-by-Step Solution: The \( z \)-score is \( \frac{47 - 44}{3} = 1 \).

Problem (Hard): A cumulative frequency distribution \( C(q) \) has \( Q_1 = 15 \), median \( 25 \), and \( Q_3 = 38 \). Calculate the spread \( \text{IQR}(C) = Q_3 - Q_1 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: From the cumulative frequency curve, \( Q_3 - Q_1 = 38 - 15 = 23 \).

rows.en: Produces smaller or even negative variance for the difference of independent variables.
Always add variances of independent variables: \(\sigma_{X-Y}^2 = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2\).
Confuses the variance of the sample mean \(\sigma^2/n\) with its standard error.
Absence of sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\) is true.
Write in context: "There is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha\) level to reject \(H_0\)."

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Normal Distribution

body.en: Exam Marking Tip (Cambridge International AS Level (9709 Paper 1 / Paper 4 / Paper 5)): Always state the distribution parameters explicitly (e.g., \(X \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) or \(\bar{X} \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\)) and sketch a quick shaded bell curve before standardizing to \(z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\). This secures the method mark even if a rounding slip occurs later.

question.en: The random variable \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) satisfies \(P(X < 65) = 0.8413\) and \(P(X < 45) = 0.0228\). Find the values of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

solution.en:
Standardising: \(\Phi\left(\frac{65 - \mu}{\sigma}\right) = 0.8413 \Rightarrow \frac{65 - \mu}{\sigma} = 1.0\), so \(65 - \mu = \sigma\).
For the lower tail: \(P(X < 45) = 0.0228 \Rightarrow \Phi\left(\frac{45 - \mu}{\sigma}\right) = 0.0228 \Rightarrow \frac{45 - \mu}{\sigma} = -2.0\), so \(\mu - 45 = 2\sigma\).
Adding the two equations: \(65 - 45 = 3\sigma \Rightarrow 20 = 3\sigma \Rightarrow \sigma = 6.67\). Then \(\mu = 65 - 6.67 = 58.33\).

question.en: [Practice 3 · Easy] In a two-stage probability tree for events \( L \) and \( M \), \( P(L) = 0.4 \) and \( P(M \mid L) = 0.7 \). Calculate the expected frequency \( q = 100 \cdot P(L \cap M) \) in \( 100 \) independent trials.

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Normal Distribution and start from \( L \).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( P(L \cap M) = 0.4 \times 0.7 = 0.28 \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: Since \( P(L \cap M) = 0.4 \times 0.7 = 0.28 \), the expected count in 100 trials is \( 28 \).
